I scored A higher on every criterion. The decisive difference is streaming. A truly streams the reply and redacts chunk by chunk with a check that is correct by construction. B waits for the whole turn to finish and then splits the finished reply into tokens. I could not run either codebase, so everything below comes from reading the code and tests.

**A**

- **Streaming:** A streams for real. `/chat` and `/chat/stream` use the same event generator (`A/app/application/services/chat.py:56-106`). `/chat` just consumes it, so the two endpoints cannot disagree.
- **Split PII:** `StreamingRedactor` (`A/app/domain/pii.py:63-107`) only releases text at a whitespace that does not follow a digit or `)`. Emails never contain whitespace, and every space inside a phone match follows a digit or `)`. So releasing text in pieces gives the same result as redacting the whole text. Tests check this for every two-way split and for one character at a time (`A/tests/test_pii.py:87,97`), and over the API at chunk sizes 1–7 (`A/tests/test_chat_stream_api.py:83`).
- **Design:** Domain, application ports and services, infrastructure and API are cleanly separated. There are repository protocols for both stores, and sessions are keyed by tenant through `SessionKey` (`A/app/domain/conversation.py:22`). Tenant prompts and limits are handled by caching one compiled agent per configuration (`A/app/infrastructure/services/deep_agent.py:44`), which is simple to follow.
- **Bug:** the tool-call limit is set only on the top-level agent (`A/app/infrastructure/services/deep_agent.py:80-86`). Tool calls made inside a subagent (the deepagents `task` tool) are not counted, so a turn can make more than N tool calls. No test covers this.

**B**

- **Streaming:** `/chat/stream` runs the whole turn first, then splits the finished reply into words with a regex and sends those as tokens (`B/app/main.py:209-216`). This meets the letter of the contract, since joined tokens equal the reply and redaction holds trivially. But nothing reaches the client until the agent is done, and the split-PII case is never really exercised.
- **Tool-call limit:** B handles this better than A. A shared per-turn budget, kept in a context variable, is checked before every tool call. The general-purpose subagent is declared explicitly with the same middleware (`B/app/agent.py:88-97`, `B/app/guardrails.py:277-329`). It is tested at `B/tests/test_api.py:250` and `B/tests/test_tenant_policies.py:297`.
- **Tenant prompts:** a context-variable middleware lets one agent serve every tenant, which is neat but less obvious to a newcomer.
- **Design:** routes, schemas, the admin router factory and the chat orchestration all live inside `create_app` closures in `B/app/main.py` (243 lines). `run_chat` catches every `Exception` and turns it into a 502 (`B/app/main.py:169`). `TurnResult` is a mutable dataclass carrying a `blocked` flag and plain dicts for guardrails (`B/app/agent.py:106-112`).
- **Tests:** they are good. The script table at `B/tests/test_memory_and_streaming.py:363-400` checks stream against chat across ten scenarios. However, because B buffers the whole turn, no test drives a chunked model stream.
